approach: A first contact for a true beginner: where Spanish is spoken, how its five vowels sound, and a handful of first words heard and said aloud, then used in tiny exchanges.
coverage: Spanish is an official language of 20 countries, plus Puerto Rico
The United States has one of the largest Spanish-speaking populations in the world
Spanish is written much as it sounds: five vowels, one short clean sound each
The letter h is silent: hola sounds like OH-lah
First words: hola, adiós, gracias, amigo, amiga, sí, no
Amigo is a male friend, amiga a female friend
Questions and exclamations open with an upside-down mark: ¿...? and ¡...!

blocks.purpose: Opens the course by placing Spanish on the map and in the learner's own country before any word is taught.

paragraphs: Spanish (español, also called castellano) is the first language of close to 500 million people. It is an official language in 20 countries, and in Puerto Rico.

You do not have to travel to hear it. In the United States, about 43 million people speak Spanish at home, and millions more speak it as a second language. You will hear it at work, in stores, on the radio and next door.

sections.heading: Where it is spoken
paragraphs: Most Spanish-speaking countries are in the Americas: Mexico, all of Central America except Belize, much of the Caribbean, and nine countries in South America. Spain is in Europe and Equatorial Guinea is in Africa.
One big exception in South America: Brazil speaks Portuguese, not Spanish.

blocks.purpose: Teaches the five vowel sounds and the silent h, the keys to reading Spanish aloud.

data.anchor: Spanish has five vowels, a e i o u, and each one makes one short, clean sound almost every time you see it.
prerequisites: a sounds like the a in "father": casa (KAH-sah).
e sounds like the e in "met": mesa (MEH-sah).
i sounds like the ee in "see": sí (see).
o sounds like the o in "or", short, with no "w" at the end: no (noh).
u sounds like the oo in "food": uno (OO-noh).
The letter h is always silent: hola is OH-lah.

blocks.purpose: Confronts the most common first mistake: pronouncing the silent h of hola.

data.question: How does hola begin when you say it?
choices: With a breathy English h: HOH-lah
With a hard j sound: JOH-lah

trapReasons.1: English pronounces the h in "hello", so it feels natural to do it here too.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: English speakers read the letter h the English way. In Spanish the h is a spelling letter only; it is never pronounced.
data.correctReasoning: Drop the h and start on the vowel: hola is OH-lah. The same goes for hotel (oh-TEL) and hospital (ohs-pee-TAHL).
data.recoveryTip: When a Spanish word starts with h, cover the h with your finger and read what is left.

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the feedback and try again.

byOption.a: Gracias is thank you. Nothing has happened yet to thank them for.
byOption.b: No answers a question. Start with a greeting.
byOption.c: Yes: hola is the everyday hello, right for a first greeting.
byOption.d: Adiós is goodbye. Save it for when you leave.

checks.prompt: Which of these South American countries does NOT have Spanish as its main language?
checks.rationale: Brazil speaks Portuguese; Colombia, Chile and Ecuador are all Spanish-speaking countries.
checks.hint: The largest country in South America speaks a different language.

checks.prompt: A coworker holds the door open for you. Which word do you say to them?
checks.rationale: Gracias means thank you, the right reply to a kindness; hola greets, adiós says goodbye, and amiga means a female friend.
Hola is the everyday Spanish hello. It is spelled with an h that is never pronounced.
checks.hint: It starts with a silent letter: OH-lah.

checks.prompt: The Spanish vowel i (as in sí) sounds like the vowel in which English word?
checks.rationale: Spanish i is always the "ee" sound of see; it is never the short i of sit or the "eye" sound of sigh.
checks.hint: Spanish vowels keep one sound. Think of sí.
